title: Machine Design
tagline: Static failure theories, fatigue, shafts, bearings, gears, fasteners and welded joints, springs, clutches, brakes, belts and chains
summary: Machine design sizes the components that make machines work so that they neither break nor wear out too soon. Building on mechanics of materials, the course covers failure theories for static loading, fatigue under fluctuating loads, and the design and selection of shafts, rolling and journal bearings, gears, threaded fasteners and welded joints, springs, and clutches, brakes, belts and chains.
overview: Machine design is the discipline that transforms the stresses, deflections, and fatigue limits of mechanics of materials into the geometry, tolerances, and material specifications of real components. The course begins with the failure theories that tell the engineer when a component is about to yield or fracture: the maximum shear stress (Tresca) and distortion energy (von Mises) criteria for ductile materials, the maximum normal stress and Mohr-Coulomb criteria for brittle materials, and the stress concentration factors that turn a nominal stress into a peak stress. These theories are the foundation on which every subsequent lesson builds, and the foundation is the reason the engineer can size a shaft, select a bearing, or specify a bolt without guessing.

The second group of lessons covers the components that rotate: shafts, bearings, and gears. The shaft is sized by the ASME equation, which combines the bending moment and the torque into an equivalent moment and then solves for the diameter. The bearing is selected by the L10 life equation, which relates the applied load to the basic dynamic load rating and the desired life. The gear is rated by the Lewis bending equation and the Hertzian contact stress, which together determine whether the tooth will break at the root or pit at the surface. These three components are the heart of every gearbox, and the gearbox is the reason the machine can change speed and torque.

The third group of lessons covers the components that join, store, and transmit: fasteners, springs, clutches, brakes, belts, and chains. The bolted joint is designed by the preload and joint stiffness model, which determines how much of the external load is carried by the bolt and how much by the joint. The spring is designed by the Wahl-corrected stress and the Goodman fatigue criterion. The clutch and brake are designed by the friction torque and the thermal capacity. The belt and chain are designed by the Euler-Eytelwein equation and the fatigue life. These components are the reason the machine can be assembled, can store energy, and can transmit power over a distance.

Throughout the course, the emphasis is on the calculation, not the rule of thumb. Every lesson includes worked examples with verified numerical answers, exercises with check values, and derivations that show where the formulas come from. The student who completes this course will be able to size a complete gearbox — shaft, bearings, gears, keys, and housing — and justify every dimension with a calculation.
outcomes: Apply the Tresca, von Mises, and Mohr-Coulomb failure theories to size a component under static loading
Construct and interpret S-N curves, apply Marin modifying factors, and use the Goodman and Gerber criteria for fluctuating stresses
Size a shaft using the ASME equation, check its deflection and critical speed, and design the key and keyway
Select a rolling bearing by the L10 life equation and analyse a journal bearing using the Sommerfeld number
Rate a gear using the Lewis bending equation and the Hertzian contact stress, and check the pitting and bending safety factors
Design a bolted joint by calculating the preload, joint stiffness, and fatigue safety factor using the Goodman criterion
Design a helical compression spring by calculating the rate, the Wahl-corrected stress, and the fatigue safety factor
Size a clutch, brake, belt, or chain drive by calculating the torque capacity, heat generation, and fatigue life

chapters.title: Failure under static loading
chapters.summary: Failure theories for ductile and brittle materials — maximum shear stress, distortion energy and Mohr–Coulomb — and stress concentration.

chapters.title: Fatigue failure
chapters.summary: S–N curves, endurance limits and modifying factors, fluctuating stresses with the Goodman and Gerber criteria, and cumulative damage.

chapters.title: Shafts and shaft components
chapters.summary: Shaft layout, stresses and deflections under combined loads, critical speeds, keys and couplings.

chapters.title: Rolling and journal bearings
chapters.summary: Rolling-bearing life, load ratings and selection, and the hydrodynamic lubrication of journal bearings.

chapters.title: Gear design
chapters.summary: Gear geometry and force analysis of meshes, bending and contact stresses in gear teeth, and gear rating.

chapters.title: Fasteners and welded joints
chapters.summary: Threaded fasteners, bolt preload and joint stiffness, and bolted, welded and bonded joints under static and fatigue loads.

chapters.title: Mechanical springs
chapters.summary: Helical compression, extension and torsion springs: stresses, deflection, buckling, fatigue and surge.

chapters.title: Clutches, brakes, belts and chains
chapters.summary: Friction clutches and brakes with their energy dissipation and temperature rise, and power transmission by belts and chains.

history.title: Coulomb's friction law
history.detail: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb publishes the law of friction, which becomes the foundation of clutch, brake, and belt design.

history.title: Thomas Tredgold's machinery
history.detail: Thomas Tredgold publishes 'Elements of Machinery', the first English-language textbook on machine design, covering shafts, gears, and bearings.

history.title: Wohler's fatigue experiments
history.detail: August Wohler begins his systematic fatigue experiments on railway axles in Berlin, establishing the S-N curve and the endurance limit.

history.title: Lewis bending equation
history.detail: Wilfred Lewis publishes the bending equation for gear teeth, the first quantitative gear design equation.

history.title: Griffith's fracture theory
history.detail: A.A. Griffith publishes the energy-based fracture theory, which explains why brittle materials fail at stresses far below their theoretical strength.

history.title: AGMA gear standard
history.detail: The American Gear Manufacturers Association publishes the first gear design standard, extending the Lewis equation to account for dynamic load, load distribution, and size.

history.title: Miner's cumulative damage rule
history.detail: M.A. Miner publishes his linear cumulative damage rule, which allows the engineer to calculate the fatigue life under variable amplitude loading.

history.title: Shigley's machine design textbook
history.detail: Joseph Shigley publishes 'Mechanical Engineering Design', which becomes the standard machine design textbook for the next six decades.
